speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not expected to say anything more in connection with manpower, but because of the amendment that has been moved I think I should say a few words at this time. I was much impressed with the speech yesterday of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) and I should like to congratulate him upon what I think was a very fair speech. I may have provoked him but I admire him for the fact that he took it in good part. No doubt he has had criticism behind the curtains and in the lobby, but he gave a most constructive speech in a fair

The Address-Mr. Cruickshank and able manner. I only wish I had the extensive knowledge of military affairs possessed by the hon. gentleman.
The government might do well to take a little advice from hon. members who have had experience, such as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and the member for Nanaimo. We happen to be fortunate in this house in having two men who could not have reached the rank or obtained the decorations they did without outstanding military ability.
I think everyone knows what I said the other day about manpower and the reserve army, but lest there be any misunderstanding on the matter I should like to quote from page 204 of Hansard of February 8 as follows:
I say tonight that I believe we should have compulsory service for the reserve army.
Then in the next column:
That is as far as I can go. I have made my stand here tonight with respect to compulsory service, so far as the reserve army is concerned.
I could go on to conscription, and probably I had better have that on the record as well. I said, and I quote from page 205 of Hansard:
My stand on conscription, when speaking before the Legion, as it is tonight, is that I think it neither desirable nor practicable nor necessary at this time.
I still think that. I am perfectly satisfied with the stand taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as to what action will be taken if and when it is necessary. I should like to go back to June 16, 1942, and quote what was said then by the Prime Minister, as follows:
I am convinced that we all want to win the war and that we are all prepared to submit to any measure which may be absolutely necessary. No thinking person can therefore have any objection to the government resorting to conscription for overseas service in the event of absolute necessity.
I did not have the privilege of hearing the Prime Minister when he spoke at the opening of this session, but I have read his speech in Hansard. The rest of you probably heard him speak. I think he made it perfectly clear just what would be done in so far as manpower is concerned if and when it was absolutely necessary to have conscription for the safeguarding of our country. Perhaps we on this side of the house should have more confidence in the Prime Minister than those on the other side. Frankly, I would not be here nor would ninety per cent of the members on this side if it were not for the leader we had. Make no mistake about that.
I have every confidence that if and when the need should arise he will not fail to take whatever steps are necessary. I am still of the opinion that some action should be taken in connection with the reserve army. With all respect to them, I perhaps do not have as much confidence in the reserve army


as some hon. members do. But if we are to have a reserve army they should have sufficient manpower with which to work. We should not have the situation referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) of five officers and four men on parade.
I am afraid we are not going to obtain the necessary results by voluntary methods. But greater efforts should be made to get men into the reserve army. I know in my own district these men could meet certain nights in the week and spend more time in the summer with their training.
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) said the other day, and for once I agree with him, that there is no reason why the boys attending college or high school should not be getting training. I know that in my district, which is the purest district in the Dominion of Canada, these boys would be better off if they were taking reserve army training two or three nights a week. This would not be training for the benefit of Canada, for the benefit of their own province or for the benefit of their own riding, it would be training to save their whole way of life. They would be much better off getting that training than attending dances, going to bowling alleys, or following the more enjoyable pursuit we have in western Canada called parking.
I appreciate that it is perhaps not practicable to carry on reserve army training in all parts of Canada at all times of the year. I do not know how it could be done in many parts of Saskatchewan at this time of the year, nor do I think it would be practicable in the northern parts of my own province. I am willing to concede that.
I believe that some method could and should be adopted to augment the services of the reserve army. I know that what I am going to say might not meet the approval of some people. Certain papers might give me a little more favourable report if I took a different stand to that which I take at the present time. During the last war I had the experience of being present in the house during the special session when we had to decide the question of manpower. It would take too long to go through the whole story but I suggest to hon. members that they check what happened in Hansard. Once more I am losing all the Hansards I have around here, but if they will check what I said on page 6868 of Hansard for December 6, 1944, they will see the stand I took at that time, and I have exactly the same opinion now. I hope some of the new members will take the trouble to look it up.

I had. to go against my party at that time, together with two other colleagues. I sat in the rump then, and after I was through speaking I had the great honour of the prime minister of the day coming over, tapping me on the shoulder, and sitting down with me behind the curtain and talking with me for half an hour. I was told by older members that, so far as they could remember, it was the first time it had happened in the history of the house. Usually prime ministers do not cross to the rump to talk to backbenchers. Afterwards we shook hands but nobody knows yet what the then prime minister and I talked about for that period of time.
I still believe that some form of compulsory service could be put into effect to strengthen the reserve army. If the Department of National Defence would become modernized and live in the age in which we are living, I believe there would be a far greater number of voluntary enlistments in the regular army. I had the privilege of accompanying the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) when he visited our part of the country. I do not say this from a partisan point of view but I do not believe that we have ever had a harder working, more able and conscientious minister than the present one. I think I know something about such matters. I did not say it before but I think I know something about soldiering. I accompanied the minister to the airport within my riding. Incidentally, it is as fine an airport as we have in Canada, and I am also of the opinion that our engineering camp is the finest in Canada.
I pointed out to the minister one little thing he could do to encourage enlistment in that very camp. At the present time there are some 200 houses for married men; the government is in the real estate business and rents the houses to them. The government should not be in the real estate business, and I believe that the Department of National Defence should cut the rent of those houses in half tomorrow, particularly for those soldiers who are privates. We should not attempt to make money through renting houses to men who want to enlist and make it their life's work. One man at that camp who did not have the advantage of an education is now spending $2 an hour two nights a week from his own pocket to increase his knowledge of mathematics so as to improve his position in the service. He has two small children, and after he has finished his army work for the day he works five nights a week in a service station in order to support his family. When such men will enlist in the regular army, surely the government can get
The Address-Mr. Cruickshank out of the real estate business, cut the rent and make enlistment more attractive to them.
There are many other ways in which we can make it more attractive. I was very glad to see that we have reduced our so-called standard for officers. If, God forbid, another war should come I hope the Department of National Defence will take their officers from the ranks as we did in the first great war and not men from the Moler barber college, Wellesley college, Rhodes scholars, and, so on. I hope they will take men who qualify for promotion on the battlefronts, as was the case in the first great war.
I want to be brief because I have spoken on this matter before. I said I would support the Canadian Legion's demand for compulsory service in the reserve army. I will support it if the matter can be brought before me in the form that the Legion desires it. My good friends over there, quite sincerely from their point of view, moved an amendment which in my opinion does not represent the desires of the Canadian Legion at all. Let me tell you what I think about it. I think it would just bring about another-and I will use the word although some people do not like it- zombie army and divide Canada as it has never been divided before. It would not be an army that could go and defend us if and when it should become necessary. As another speaker has said, those who moved the amendment have not adopted the attitude they should have. We do not want to have a war in Ontario, British Columbia or Quebec. If we have to fight a war we want to fight it as far away as we can, and we want reinforcements suitable for that purpose.
As I understand it, the amendment would just mean the creation of another zombie army. We would have nothing but dissatisfaction. We know from experience that in the past we could not get such men to even go up to the Aleutians. We know that we had trouble to try to get them on the boats to go over as reinforcements. Therefore let us not divide Canada again in this critical time. Another point brought out yesterday was that we are endeavouring to secure sufficient reinforcements for our armed forces in Korea and possibly elsewhere. In my opinion you can never obtain the reinforcements if you take what available manpower there is and put it by compulsion in another zombie army. That is all such an army would amount to. If we follow that course we will not have reinforcements available. We will not have men for the air force which, as every member with any military knowledge knows, would be the most important part of our armed forces if and when another war comes. The air arm is the force to which we will have to look.

The Address-Mr. Beyerstein We can never secure airmen by compulsion. Any military man knows that. If we drain off the available manpower for another reserve army for service in Canada only I believe we will defeat the very end that every hon. member in all good faith intends to support.
I wanted to make my stand clear, and I still stand by what I said before. If it is possible in any way to recruit strength for the reserve army now-not for defence in Canada only-I would support it. As it is, I am going to oppose the amendment to the amendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks in this debate will be very brief. I merely wish to take this opportunity to endorse what has already been said by other members of our group concerning the necessity of implementing price and wage controls, and the necessity for supporting a preparedness program for the defence of Canada. The subject of price controls was thoroughly covered by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) when he spoke in this debate a few days ago; therefore it is not necessary for me to deal further with it at this time. I merely wish to endorse the facts that he presented when he spoke.
I should like to take a few moments, however, to discuss the question of preparedness in case of a national emergency. I feel that we should give full support to the preparedness program submitted by the Canadian Legion. At the present time the government leaders seem to have divided opinions concerning a program of national preparedness. For example, I have here a clipping from the Calgary Herald of December 30, 1950, which quotes the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as having said:
The situation is of course very serious, but I have said a good many times that I didn't expect to live long enougli to see another world war-and I haven't changed my view.
One has no way of determining how long the Prime Minister intends to live, but in view of the statements of some of the other ministers one may conclude that the Prime Minister was either talking for home consumption or he has lost hope of living to a very great age. On February 8, 1951, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) took part in this debate, and at page 179 of Hansard had this to say:
Since parliament met last autumn, world events have moved swiftly. Canada, with the rest of the free world, has had to revise its schedule of preparedness. The challenge of aggressive communism leaves no choice but to move ahead at once, and quickly, with defence preparations planned on a scale never before contemplated except in time of all-out war.


I think that statement gives us a clearer picture of what we are facing at the present time, so I think there can be no doubt about the reasonableness and soundness of the program which has been presented by the Canadian Legion. 1 say there should be no delay in adopting that program. The Legion program, "Operation preparedness", consists of three parts. The first point is a request for national registration. I agree with the Legion that it is necessary to efficiently organize the resources and manpower of this country. The value of national registration in connection with the control of aliens and subversive elements was demonstrated in world war II, and I believe that is a point which should be implemented at the very earliest opportunity.
The second point in the program is the mobilization of industry and resources for defence production. There is no doubt that present supplies are inadequate to meet any increased enlistment in the active and reserve forces. If this situation is allowed to continue until the need arises the ultimate result will be that our hastily mobilized forces will not only be poorly trained but will be tragically lacking in equipment with which to meet an enemy which has been trained since youth, and which would be completely ruthless. Without adequate training it would be very difficult to cope with such an enemy.
The third point in the Legion program is compulsory training in the reserve forces. We must have a definite program which will prevent a repetition of our bitter experience in world war II, when Canadian citizens were committed to battle without adequate training. I am sure not a member of this house would want to see his son in the active army. If that should ever become necessary, however, I am sure he would want his son to have training which would enable him to defend not only himself but his home and his country.
Those are the three main parts of the Legion program. I think we should endorse them wholeheartedly and lose no time in implementing them. If war should come it is highly probable that the Russians would send considerable forces to Alaska, no doubt accompanied by bands of tough Siberian troops who would be landed by air in the Canadian north. Their object in doing this would be to create confusion and alarm, in the hope that it would prevent us from sending troops and material abroad. A second purpose would be to pinpoint our attention on the defence of North America while they extended their hold on Asia and Europe, with ultimately a life and death struggle for possession of this continent. A third purpose in occupying

Alaska would be to hamper the development of our resources. The present lack of population and communications in the north country is a direct threat to the security of this continent. Even the well-advertised Alaska highway is not an all-weather military road, and that is another point which should be considered in the near future.
The problems I have mentioned are too vital to be made a political football, and I challenge the government and some members of the opposition to face the issue. There are those who believe the next war will not require armies, that it will be a push button war. Their idea is that if we have more atomic bombs than the Russians we can win a war within a few days. Those who hold that opinion should take a lesson from Hitler, who thought he could grab Russia in one short blitz. He found he could not, and failed miserably in that attempt. Hitler was surprised to find that Russia could suffer more than five million casualties in the first six months of the war and still muster sufficient forces for counter-offensives which lasted through most of the winter of 1941-42. The Russians are ruthless in their fighting and we must be prepared to meet them. There is no doubt that they would make an attempt to invade Alaska if it should reach the point of war, and I say we should be prepared to meet that emergency.
Then we must have a program of home defence; and in drawing up such a program the utmost care should be taken to come as close as possible to equality of service and sacrifice. There must be no room for such dodges or subterfuges as renting a quarter section of land, or obtaining a false certificate in business. Our program should be made as nearly equitable as possible.
These are the main points that prompted me to take part in this debate. There is one other small matter I should like to mention, however; that is the growing concern over the abolition of rent control. At present approximately a million people in Canada are under the protection of rent control. If that protection should suddenly be removed we would find that people now paying $30 to $40 a month would have their rent increased to perhaps $60 or $70. The people renting homes are usually in the lower income brackets, and cannot afford such an increase.
The cost of living index at the present time stands at 172.5, and a substantial boost in rents would make it almost unbearable for people in the lower income brackets. I was sorry to hear the announcement that probably National Housing Act loans would be curtailed this year. There is still a shortage of homes. It has been said that houses built 80709-25
The Address-Mr. Picard under the National Housing Act scheme take care of only those in the higher income brackets. However, an analysis of 15,000 houses built in 1949 shows that 55 per cent of them were for people in the middle income group, those who were receiving from $2,400 to $3,500 a year; 11 per cent of those 15,000 were built for those in the income bracket below $2,400 a year; and 34 per cent were for those with incomes over $3,500 a year. On analysing the building under the National Housing Act, it will be found that about two-thirds of the homes being built are built by those who are in the middle or lower income brackets. I therefore think it is a pity that the National Housing Act loans should be curtailed at this time, especially when there is such a great shortage of housing in Canada.
Those are the main points I wanted to discuss at this time. In closing I would urge that the government should by all means institute at this session a system of over-all price, wage and rent controls. In addition to that, they should formulate a program of preparedness similar to that suggested by the Canadian Legion, in case of a national emergency. The vote on our subamendment will show whether politics is stronger than the conviction of the individual; and I would urge everyone to support this subamendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As I
rise, Mr. Speaker, I want my first words to be ones of congratulation to the mover (Mr. McMillan) and the seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply on the ability and the dignity they showed when they performed their duties. Through you, sir, I think we might extend to Mr. Speaker the congratulations of the house on the way he represented Canada when he was in England last summer. Not only have the pictures which have reached us shown his appearance of dignity but those who were there-and other hon. members will speak with more authority than I do at the moment, because they were there-have told us of his dignity and the splendid manner in which he spoke for Canada.
I had intended, in this debate to speak on international affairs and, since this last motion, on mobilization or on manpower. But I also had in mind that something had been said in the house about one of the important functions of the house, namely that performed by the public accounts committee, of which I have been chairman for the last six years. I therefore thought it might be appropriate at this time for me to avail myself of this opportunity to say a few words on the matter.
The public accounts committee is one of the means at the disposal of parliament by which it may exercise control of the expenditure
386	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Picard of public moneys. By "control" I mean the ascertaining of whether the moneys voted by parliament have been wisely spent or wisely used. To quote Durell, at page 117:
. . . the functions of the committee extend, however, beyond the formality of the expenditure to its "wisdom, faithfulness and economy." It should not only act as a check upon extravagant, irregular or unauthorized expenditure, but also, within limits, upon unwise methods of management.
I therefore cannot let go without comment some of the remarks that have been made in this house by some hon. members opposite in the C.C.F. party to the effect that the public accounts committee had not discharged its duties properly. I think that the importance of the house exercising control over public expenditures is such that public confidence in the committee must be safeguarded and kept, so that the public will feel that the committee is performing its duty in the right manner. I therefore propose to devote a few minutes to that question. Then I shall make way for others who may want, at this late stage in the debate, to take part in it.
If we refer to our own House of Commons rules we find in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms that the only reference made to the committee on public accounts is on page 177. Standing order 63, paragraph 1, reads in part as follows:
At the commencement of each session, a special committee, consisting of five members, shall be appointed, whose duty it shall be to prepare and report, with all convenient speed, lists of members to compose the following standing committees of the house:
. . . (e) On public accounts, to consist of 50 members, 15 of whom shall constitute a quorum.
In the past the custom has been for the government first to appoint the striking committee or committee that prepares the list of members. Then the custom has been to appoint the different committees and subsequently to present a motion to this effect:
That the standing committees of this house shall severally be empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may be referred to them by the house, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records.
As to the public accounts committee, the tradition has been that the main thing would be to refer to them the report of the Auditor General and the public accounts of the current year. This has been the practice up until now. The committees were usually formed immediately after the address in reply was adopted. Each year up until now this procedure has been followed, and the committee has been appointed and the public accounts have been referred to them. On the other hand, the committee has not sat each year for the last twenty-five years. In the past the custom has been for a member of the committee to write to the chairman or to get in
fMr. Picard.l

touch with him and to suggest that the committee should assemble or to suggest a subject for the work of the committee. In the past twenty-two years the committee has sat only eight times, four of them under my chairmanship. The committee sat in 1929 under the chairmanship of the then hon. member for Cartier, Mr. Sam Jacobs. The committee reported but made no recommendations. It held eleven meetings and heard twelve witnesses, but made no recommendations whatsoever. The committee sat again in 1939, and everybody will remember its object at that time. It conducted what has been called the Bren gun inquiry. Suffice it for me to mention the name. The committee was in the middle of its sittings when the house rose and it did not report. The committee sat for the next time in 1943.
I should say that in 1939 they sat under the chairmanship of Mr. William Fraser. They sat again in 1943 under the chairmanship of Mr. Fraser. They reported after a few meetings, but made no recommendations. The committee sat in 1944, again under Mr. Fraser. They sat four times and made no report. The committee sat in 1945 for the first time under my chairmanship. The committee met informally on November 9, before any work had been referred to it, at the request of the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth). At that time nothing had been referred to it and the matter suggested for study by the hon. member was an account for the current year, and not an account that was reported in the public accounts.
The chairman ruled that that matter should be brought to the attention of the war expenditures committee that was still in existence during that year. The committee then sat in 1947, again under my chairmanship, although for a few meetings it was under the chairmanship of Mr. Isnor, now Senator Isnor. Twenty-eight meetings were held. Besides the usual perfunctory reports, the committee made five reports of a constructive nature, two of which were over the signature of my colleague, Mr. Isnor, and three over my own.
First of all, the committee studied Bill No. 22 and reported favourably thereon. The committee then studied the question of the Japanese evacuees on the British Columbia coast. It made a thorough study of the problem and made a constructive report on it. The committee also made a study of the administration of the custodian of enemy property concerning the so-called illegal organizations in Canada, and we also reported on the matter.

The committee also heard the Auditor General on the memorandum that he had prepared especially as to his suggestions concerning different aspects of his report; and finally the committee studied the building projects under the Veterans Land Act, administered under the Department of Veterans Affairs, on which the committee reported.
In passing I might note that I as chairman had to make the first draft of three of these reports, and if any hon. member might feel that I was biased and was trying to cover up or protect the government, as has been said by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), I might say that in the fifth report, the one concerning the building projects, I was the one who first included a word of censure against the gentleman who was administering that branch. Although he had been a very efficient man in other quarters, I and other members of the committee on all sides of the house considered that he had not shown enough ability in carrying the job he held in charge of the building projects for the veterans. The department evidently took this into consideration because the next summer he was moved to another position owing to the fact that he had previously proven his worth in other endeavours.
In 1949 the committee held only two meetings, and heard the Auditor General. The general elections interrupted the sittings of the committee, with the result that is quite evident in this house at present.
Then the committee sat in 1950, which is the year which has been the object of criticism by some hon. members opposite. The committee held thirty-two meetings, which was the first time in a great many years that the committee had shown such activity. The committee heard seventeen witnesses and presented five constructive reports. When I say "constructive" I do not say it only to be complimentary to the committee, but to signify that they were not only routine reports, which are often made, but rather reports that dealt with conditions that had been brought to the attention of the committee, reports which will have an effect either on the presentation of estimates or, as I have been informed lately, may have an effect on the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, a review of which is to be presented to parliament.
The committee first presented a report on the relationship of estimates to public accounts. It then presented a report on the study of the Auditor General's report. It then went on to report on the sale by the War Assets Corporation to Canadair Limited of property at Cartierville, Quebec. It
80709-25g
The Address-Mr. Picard reported on the sale by War Assets Corporation to Canadian Exploration of Emerald lake, and finally it dealt with other aspects of War Assets Corporation.
Hon. members of the C.C.F. party have thought fit at this session or at the last fall session, or at the end of the previous session, to cast aspersions on the work of the committee and on the chairman. I would not take the trouble to rise if only my humble person was concerned in such a question; but I think the public accounts committee performs one of the most important duties that this house has to perform. I think that the confidence of the public of Canada in its members is most important to our democratic institutions; therefore at this moment I think I ought to tell the facts as to that and present a true picture of the situation to the house to show that really the committee has worked assiduously, and has opened as far as it could the doors to every member to investigate, to question and to do whatever they wanted to do on the different matters that were brought before the committee.
Last fall during the short session a gentleman whom I personally respect highly, namely, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), said this, as quoted at page 632 of Hansard:
The public accounts committee met and we were sidetracked most cleverly into considering the form of the estimates. Ninety per cent of the time of the committee was spent in determining the form in which the estimates should be presented at the next session of parliament.
Except for the fact that I object to the word "sidetracked", and except for the fact of the proportion of ninety per cent, there is something in this. We studied the form of the estimates, but we were not sidetracked into it as I shall show in a moment. It was the committee itself, and the committee with the approval of all members sitting there and without any protest to us, that decided to hear the Auditor General and get whatever memorandum he wished to bring before us. It was not the committee that decided that the Auditor General should come before us and take the estimates. We decided unanimously in the steering committee or the agenda committee when a representative of the other party, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), for whom I also have great respect, was there, and who was more or less responsible, more than anybody else, for the committee assembling on that day, because he was the one who had written to me asking that the committee should assemble. He asked that because it was his intention to put before the committee a proposal to the effect

The Address-Mr. Picard that the committee should reconsider reviewing the affairs of, or the moneys spent by, the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and the Department of National Defence.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North sent that letter to me, and I immediately assembled the committee. I might say here that that gentleman was made one of the members of the agenda committee. He brought in his proposal. At that time the hon. member for Halifax proposed that we should go into a different type of study. If I may be permitted, I shall quote from the minutes and proceedings of the public accounts committee of April 27, which says:
The chairman stated that the subcommittee had decided to call Mr. Sellar as the first witness. It had been agreed that Mr. Sellar would read a brief, on which he would be questioned, and that when this had been disposed of, the committee would proceed to consideration of the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year 1948-49.
Then if I turn to the verbatim report itself, I find I said at the time that the committee on agenda had decided that:
Mr. Sellar be asked first to come before us and to present whatever brief he might feel advisable to submit; and in connection with that, it was agreed that we would not interrupt Mr. Sellar while he was reading his submission but afterwards we would limit our questions to the brief itself, and that then he would go ahead and submit the other material which he wants to place before the committee, and that when he had concluded his submissions the material would be open for discussion. Consideration of the report of the Auditor General itself would be the next order of business. Following that Mr. Stewart suggested that at the conclusion of Mr. Sellar's examination the committee review the accounts of the Department of National Defence as set forth in the public accounts for the fiscal year 1948-49. Mr. Isnor suggested that the superintendent of insurance of the Department of Finance and the director of the annuities branch of the Department of Labour be examined by the committee as to the facilities of their branches. The subcommittee recommended that for the present we would limit ourselves to a study of the report of the Auditor General and subsequently that a further meeting of the steering committee would be held to decide as to the matters that will be taken up.
At that meeting, when this was given as the order of precedence by the chairman, were present the two gentlemen who later in the house criticized by saying they had been sidetracked in considering the question of estimates. Both the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) were there at that time; yet I find no word in the proceedings indicating that they protested in any way by suggesting that some other matter be considered immediately.
I have here a note where the present hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) asked what the order of business would be,


following which the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) spoke. It appears from the record that everyone agreed that should be the order of business at that time. No member rose to his feet and said that he had been sidetracked into doing something he did not want to do. No one objected. Indeed the whole committee approved of that order of business. That was why we called the Auditor General to appear before us. We did not dictate to the Auditor General as to what he should tell us. Here is a man who has been appointed and who, because of a regulation, is, except upon a two-thirds vote of the members of the House of Commons, immune from discharge from his office. Without that vote we can do nothing to him. He is above politics, and during most of the years he has been there has been free in his language, as have his predecessors.
I know of some hon. members on all sides of the house who have thought that, at times, he has expressed his views a little too openly respecting matters of policy. So we cannot say that this man came to that committee with any idea given to him by anyone as to how he should treat this matter or the other. For years the Auditor General had had certain pet ideas as to the way estimates should be presented. He came to us this year and gave us the benefit of his memorandum.
I do not think it would have been fair to the treasury officials, to the comptroller of the treasury or to the House of Commons if we had been satisfied just to listen to the Auditor General and then to have said, "Sir, you are a most important fellow. We will accept whatever you have decided. Let us now move to the next order of business."
In our committee we proceeded in the order I have indicated. Hon. members from all sides questioned the gentleman as to the advisability of his recommendations, some of which were reflected later on in our report, and with some of which we did not agree. We expressed our views upon them. I do not think it would be fair to say that anyone was sidetracked into studying the estimates instead of going into the public accounts.
Later on I shall discuss the question of what should be the order of business in such a committee; but I do object strenuously- especially when it comes from a man so mild in manner, so pleasant and one whom I admire so much as the hon. member for Melfort. I am quite sure he overstated it and did not accurately express his views when he said, "We were sidetracked." He may have felt we should have done something else and, if so, he is free to have his opinion and I will respect it. But when

The Address-Mr. Picard
he says that he was sidetracked, when no objection had come from anywhere, I must object.
Further than that, it is true that we spent a third-not ninety per cent- of our time dealing with the form of the estimates. We spent fourteen out of thirty-two meetings in that work. The evidence to which I have just referred shows that at the time the subcommittee reported no one thought he was being sidetracked, or that anything wrong was being done.
I did not bring with me the large volume of Hansard for last year in which the speech of the hon. member for Moose Jaw appears. However, he repeated almost verbatim the same speech at this session and, for that reason, I felt it unnecessary to bring the large volume to my desk in the chamber. The result is that I have only his words delivered this session, which are sufficient to give an idea of what his views were in committee, and the criticisms he made. In his speech at this session he said:
When we got into the committee, although the members asked for a good deal of information they were not able to get it.
Which is false.
Opposition members asked for witnesses, they asked for figures, and they asked for the public accounts. They asked for many things, but they did not get much satisfaction. We were repeatedly overruled when we sought information, and we were consistently refused the public accounts themselves. I think that the committee sat for three months before it even got to the public accounts.
Well, that is what I call misrepresentation. That is a misleading statement, if there is such a thing. The committee followed the procedure that had been approved by all members of the steering committee who were present. I do not think it is fair to spread throughout the country the suggestion that a committee such as that, the function of which is to control government expenditures, to make sure nothing is wrong with expenditures, and to decide whether proper amounts have been spent, or if expenditures have been made wisely, has misbehaved for political reasons, or that it has failed to help our democratic institutions, as our friends profess to do.
When they say we have spoken too much about estimates, I would refer them to a book that was issued by the treasury in Great Britain. It is for official use, and is called "Parliamentary Supply Procedure".
Item 11 at page 7 states:
It has long been the established usage that important changes in the form of the estimates should not be made or sanctioned by the treasury without their first being submitted to and approved by the public accounts committee.
The Auditor General had suggestions to make. We did not necessarily have to accept them. We recognized his competence over us in matters of accountancy. We recognized that he had a much better grasp of many of those economical and financial problems than we have. Yet, no matter what our way of thinking might have been we had to judge by what we had in our own minds. We could not accept all he said without looking into it carefully. I think there were on the committee enough men of good sense to judge fairly and who were able to assess the value of those suggestions, for the benefit of the public of Canada, to assure the control by parliament in respect of whatever the gentleman might have suggested.
In the same booklet I find this:
-since the form of the estimates directly affects the parliamentary control of expenditure and is intimately connected with the form of the appropriation accounts, the treasury has undertaken to consult the public accounts committee before making or sanctioning important changes of form.
I think it was important that the committee should look into that carefully and a number of sittings were given up to the consideration of that question. I think I can say without divulging any secret that the form in which the estimates will be presented this year will reflect many of the suggestions made last year by the committee. I think the results will satisfy one of two of the hon. members who criticized namely, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) when he sees that our many suggestions were not ignored but were looked into and even incorporated in the new form of the estimates.
When the Auditor General came before us I do not think it would have been right for the committee to say that they would not consider his memorandum, that they would either approve it or reject it. I do not think the committee, in order to please the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), should have taken up the question of how many nails went into this or what material was used somewhere else. I think the committee did its duty by acting as it did.
I am given to understand that these changes will be made at this session and then I hope that hon. members will see that our work has been well done. A most misleading statement was made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw when he said that hon. members had been prevented from asking for information and that the truth had been withheld. Since we were acting under the instructions of the steering committee and were studying the form of the estimates, naturally when the Auditor General was before us we asked him what form he would like the estimates of certain departments to take. We agreed to take as an example the Department of Agriculture.

The Address-Mr. Picard We took that department, not because of any prejudice but simply because it came under "A", the first department. We asked the Auditor General how he would like to see those estimates worded or grouped in the future.
After hearing that gentleman it was our duty to hear the deputy minister of agriculture, the secretary of the treasury board, who is also an assistant deputy minister of finance, and the comptroller of the treasury. As responsible members of this house we obtained such information on the problem as we could get before making our recommendations. I think it was a normal procedure at that time for the committee not to consider whether there should be an elevator at this place or something somewhere else. We had to decide whether the groupings suggested by the Auditor General were the right ones.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw went ahead and asked questions that had nothing to do with the matter before the committee. In order to have the proceedings carried on in a proper manner, the chairman had to rule him out of order. The committee was dealing with the question submitted by the subcommittee and deciding on the form of the estimates, not on how much money should be spent on a particular item. That would come under the public accounts and would be considered later. If we had sat long enough it would have come up later on.
I agree with one suggestion that was made, that the public accounts committee should take a different department each year, look carefully into all the items and ask all the necessary pertinent questions. But I do object to the statement being made that hon. members were sidetracked and were refused information by the committee or were not given the chance to ask for figures. It is a distortion of the fact to say that figures were refused in the committee.
Everything that was pertinent was given, but when a question was out of order, when it did not concern the item under consideration, it was ruled out. I think the chairman of the committee went to great lengths to satisfy hon. members. When the brief on the estimates presented by the Auditor General was disposed of the committee continued with its work of reviewing the Auditor General's report. The report of the committee dated June 15, 1950, deals with the form of the estimates, the number of the items, the wording of the items, the details of estimates, the summary of estimates, the revenue producing services, the vote texts that legislate, the committee on estimates and the public accounts committee.


As I say, after that part of our work was completed we went into the Auditor General's report. The hon. member for Moose Jaw objected that the study of the Auditor General's report was taking up time that should have been employed in studying the public accounts. That is a most misleading statement because in considering the Auditor General's report we were dealing with the public accounts. The report of the Auditor General contains references to certain matters which under the statute he is bound to report to us and other matters to which he considers it his duty to call our attention. Here is what Durell's "Parliamentary Grants" has to say:
In the first place, in dealing with the purely accounting point of view, it (the public accounts committee) necessarily reviews the comptroller and auditor general's report and investigates any irregularities brought to notice in that report. In this respect its examination amounts to an enlarged revision of that report, supplementing it by oral examination both of the accounting officer and of other officers concerned in the expenditure. In point of fact the committee is primarily guided in its line of investigation by the comptroller and auditor general's report, as to the subjects it selects for consideration, though it is not necessarily restricted to the ground covered by that report.
I think that should suffice to show that when the committee took up the study of the Auditor General's report it was acting in a correct way. As I said, the Auditor General is obliged by statute to direct our attention to certain matters and is at liberty to bring other items of the public accounts before us. After we had studied the report of the Auditor General we submitted a second report containing five items. The first item dealt with the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act and it was stated that it should be amended to authorize writing off uncollectable debts that have accumulated up to 1940 in the government accounts. The second recommendation was that the government should consider the advisability of revising the International Boundary Waters Act.
The next paragraph stated that the committee was of the opinion that the yearly report of every crown corporation should be referred for study to a select committee of the house. The fourth recommendation was in connection with the post office guarantee fund and the fifth recommendation had to do with the Department of Public Works bearing the cost of office accommodation for all departments. The report reads:
Your committee is of the opinion that departmental heads in co-operation with treasury board officials, the comptroller of the treasury and the Auditor General should examine the advisability of charging each department in respect of the space which it occupies.

Those are important questions, and I do not see that it was wasting the time of the committee or the house to have gone into them. I contend that the committee of last session did valuable work. Before it finally adjourned it also looked into a number of matters brought to its attention by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). At that time, since the committee had already disposed of the two items which had been selected by the steering committee, it might have accepted the idea of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) to proceed right away to investigate one department of the public accounts, but we had had certain remarks by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, and had lost one full meeting investigating whether or not it was good policy to have a quinquennial census in the western provinces, and whether we might save a few pennies there.

The gentleman in charge, who should know better than my hon. friend, came before us and said it was necessary and had to be carried on. From the hon. member's performance that day I think the committee got the impression that it could do better work, work more satisfactory to the people of Canada, by investigating the three matters that had been suggested by the leader of the opposition. The committee might not have had unanimous approval in dealing with them, but I should like to emphasize that it studied them carefully and then reported. My hon. friend cannot say that the committee did1 not use its time well in so doing, and much better than it would have by accepting some of his views that it should go into this or that small question in order to save a few cents by not purchasing nails or hammers for this or that project.
I am convinced of one thing. Since I have been chairman of that committee I have always had the view-and I was fortunate in finding the same view expressed elsewhere -that the essential principle on which parliamentary control is based should not be complicated checks imposed before expenditure takes place but an orderly audit of the expenditure after it has occurred. That is the job of the Auditor General and of a committee of parliament through examination of the results of his audit. If my hon. friend had been in his seat earlier he would have heard what I said in, the first part of my remarks, and I advocate that he should read them in Hansard. I said that for the first time last year the committee sat for any length of time. It had to listen to a long brief from the Auditor General, and it was its duty to report on it.
The Address-Mr. Picard
The committee must perform the actual work of not only going into each department but also, as I suggested a moment ago, digging first into the Auditor General's report. The amount of time spent on that depends on how hon. members put their questions, how they interpret what is in the report, and how they word their questions in order to secure the answers they want. Examination of past expenditures, says Durell, is the best means of informing the House of Commons how to criticize further expenditures. I contend that the committee did valuable work last session. It followed the agenda to which no objection was raised at first by the very few hon. members who later violently criticized our work. As I pointed out a moment ago, material results will come about from the work performed. I am convinced that good results can also be achieved by the committee if the work is performd in the spirit which motivated the inception of the public accounts committee, that is, the verification of whether moneys voted have been well spent.

Anyway it will oblige the next speaker if I do so because he would not have much time to speak before six o'clock. I shall conclude in a few minutes. Another comment that is not out of place is to point out for the future-and this is directed to my hon. friend as well as to others who may want to bring different matters before the committee-that questions of policy do not come within the purview of the committee on public accounts. The other day my hon. friend said that he intended to have generals, admirals, commodores and so on called before the committee. All right. I may not be there, but it will be all right with the one who is chairman of the committee if it concerns an analysis of how moneys have been spent, but not to determine whether the money should have been voted, not to determine whether these people agree with the policy behind purchasing of these items. The function of the committee is to check on the expenditures and not on whether it was wise to decide to spend this or that. It is there to ascertain whether the money that has been spent has been well spent, whether there is something wrong or crooked about it, or whether everything is all right.
In this connection I might also quote Durell, a recognized authority on the subject

The Address-Mr. Picard in the British House of Commons and in all other commonwealth legislatures. At page 118 Durell says:
The committee is ... in no way concerned with questions of policy in the broader sense.
That would apply to any committee which had as its aim the securing from departmental officials of information as to the what-for and wherefor of the different items, and the criticizing thereof. We have a right to know where the money has gone, how much money has been spent; but whether or not it was voted or recommended wisely is not for the committee to decide. On page 119 Durell says:
The chief obstacle to discussing merit will generally be found in determining the question as to the extent to which administration is involved. The reasons for the limitation in the functions of the committee as regards policy are twofold. In the first place a discussion on questions of policy would imply the right, whether exercised or not, of approving or disapproving of that policy, and might be set up by the department in its defence. Any system, however, which would tend to relieve ministers of their responsibilities in this respect would unduly diminish the control of the executive, and might also diminish the carefulness of the department. There would consequently be insuperable objections to any attempt on the part of the House of Commons to delegate questions of policy to a committee. Ministerial responsibility is an underlying constitutional maxim, and no intervention between the minister and the House of Commons, to which alone he must answer, would be consistent with its satisfactory working. The amount of the estimates or the amount of any particular grant are matters of policy, and it would be entirely outside the scope of the committee to question either, or to investigate the grounds on which they were based. This is true generally, even when the policy is common knowledge; but it may sometimes be the case that items have been inserted in an estimate on grounds of policy based on confidential documents. As the minister could not be called on to divulge these to the house in order to justify his insertion of the items, still less could the department be called on to produce them to the committee for discussion.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that personally I believe it is rendering a disservice to our democratic institutions to cast aspersions upon the work of such a committee, especially when those aspersions are founded not on fact but on personal peevish impressions. For a number of years I have had the privilege of sitting on such committees. During the war I sat on the war expenditures committee with several hon. members of the same party to which my hon. friend belongs, members who in my opinion were as faithful to the principles of their party as my hon. friend could be, and I never heard them cast any such aspersions. As chairman of the subcommittee looking into the matter of synthetic rubber I had the opportunity of sitting with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I found him to be a gentleman who carefully

studied all questions, and I am sure he never thought I wanted to hide things, just as I never thought he wanted to do anything which would be detrimental to the country. On the war expenditures committee of 1943 which looked into the question of aluminum, I sat with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I took an active part in the work of that committee, though perhaps not such a prominent part as he took, and I do not think he ever had cause to think I was not performing my duty fully or that I was not unbiased in the way I approached that problem. Nor did I ever think he ever had any wrong intentions in asking his questions. The same thing happened in 1947, when we investigated the matters I mentioned a moment ago. On that committee we had another member of the same party, Mr. Burton. I remember very well, too, that in the war expenditures committee of 1941 or 1942 I voted with three members of the opposition parties to make sure our proceedings would be published. At the time I stated that whatever happened should be divulged, even though it should concern a friend of ours.
So, Mr. Speaker, believing it important not to myself but to parliament to deal with these aspersions that have been cast upon the work of the committee, after the care that committee took to look into the matters brought before it, I thought it my duty to rise and bring this to the attention of the house and state the facts as they really are. In doing so I believe I am performing a service, because if we are to carry on with our democratic institutions it is most important that the people should continue to have confidence in the House of Commons; not in one party in particular, because parties may come and go, but the institutions last. The moment the people become convinced that those institutions are wrong, it is not important what party may be in power; there will be no democracy then.

speechtext:
In common with all hon. members, Mr. Speaker, I feel that this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne offers us an opportunity to bring into the house the views of our constituents and also to place before the house their local problems while they are still fresh in our minds. To my mind, a member of parliament returning to Ottawa after visiting his riding comes here with a knowledge of his people, their needs and their point of view. This personal contact with one's riding makes for greater efficiency in the carrying out of our duties as members of parliament. Having in mind the value of this constituency contact, I should like to see the sessions divided into two parts, with half the session held in the early part of the year, in the spring, and the other half in the fall. This would allow members, particularly those from the west, an opportunity of going home, contacting their constituencies and coming back fresh for the fray. I would of course take it for granted that the first half of the session would be adjourned and reconvened later, in the fall of the year, with just the one indemnity. In that case there would be no extra cost to the government. This would particularly benefit all the members who come from the extreme ends of Canada. I make that as a purely personal suggestion; I have not consulted my colleagues about it; but I believe that hon. members in all parts of the house would be quite satisfied to have the sessions split in that way. Their work would have that freshness resulting from the benefit of close contact with their constituencies to which I referred. I find that matters are brought to our attention that have a great deal of merit and are worthy of consideration, as was the case during my recent visit to my own constituency; and I propose to deal with one or two of them tonight.
First of all, I shall deal briefly with the subamendment that is now before the house. We who have seen service and who understand some of the problems can readily sympathize with the point of view expressed by the Canadian Legion in pressing for compulsory service at this time. This amendment to a certain extent follows the line of argument of the Canadian Legion. I believe we have made certain commitments to the Atlantic pact group and to the United Nations with regard to the supply of manpower; and 80709-26
The Address-Mr. Jones before we could deal adequately with the proposals for compulsory service made in this subamendment, I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) this question: Are we now able, through the voluntary enlistment method, to provide all the manpower that we have been committed to supply to those two groups? I should also like to ask him:	Are we supplying all the
personnel that has been requested of us by those two groups? Of course that includes our own national defence personnel. In other words, are we prepared to meet our commitments on the voluntary basis of enlistment? These questions should be answered before we could deal with this subamendment adequately. Instead of our talking of defence and armaments continually, I believe we should hear more in this house and outside of it-through the press and through all channels of thought and action in Canada- about sound proposals for peace that will be acceptable to those who now threaten us with aggression. Not this evening but later on I should like to deal with that matter. I feel that all hon. members should give more attention to the question: Are we doing all that we can to bring about world peace or are we just so obsessed with the idea of defence and the idea that we must prepare to withstand aggression that we have overlooked the fact that there is a possible solution to our problems by expressing tolerance and a willingness to work with the possible enemy towards ultimate peace.
The frank and, I might say, courageous statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) recently has given comfort and relief to many Canadians who up to that time entertained-and justifiably so, I think -fears that the question of conscription would be sidestepped as has long been the case in the history of Canada. I agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) that the Legion brief was prepared some time before the Prime Minister made that statement and was based on the assumption that Canada would be torn by strife and turmoil should we find ourselves faced with a manpower or defence emergency, as was the case during the first and second wars. The subamendment calling for compulsory service in the reserve forces, if carried out- and I take it that their intention is complete compulsory service-would call all ablebodied men to the reserve forces. With the I.Q. requirements and the physical requirements for the reserve army much lower than those for the regular army, plus the extended age limit that covers that group, I feel that these lower standards could bring together close to 10 per cent of our population. If such be the case, we would call to the colours
