The Address-Mr. Jones
1.400.000	men. But let us say that only five per cent would be affected. In that case
700.000	men would be called up for training in the reserve forces.
I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has already pointed out our position with regard to equipment and suitable quarters. I think he showed clearly that Canada is not prepared to take care of the training of anything like 700,000 men, and possibly not even 100,000 men. I therefore feel that more thought has to be given to the suggestion of the Canadian Legion and that a -more balanced approach has to be reached before we can do anything about it. I do not think for a moment that the present reserve facilities could stand the strain of this vastly increased number of personnel. Compulsory service is a step that may have to be taken later on; and we have from the Prime Minister the assurance that should the need arise the government would put that system into effect. In the meantime, establishments and equipment of the reserve army should receive the immediate attention of the Minister of National Defence. I believe that a survey made today of the eligible men in any town in Canada, asking their reasons for not joining the reserve army on a voluntary basis, would give sufficient answers with regard to the numerous kicks and dissatisfactions that are prevalent throughout Canada about the present set-up of the reserve army so that it would give the minister a sound background of knowledge as to how to improve those conditions that are now barring the entry of men into the service, by eliminating several of the causes of complaint. I admit that some of them are trivial, but nevertheless they are causes of complaint.
Closely tied up with the subject of the reserve army is the question of civil defence.
I propose to deal briefly with this subject. It is well known to everyone that the legal responsibility for the defence of Canada is a federal one. The defence, or protection of our people from attack, the defence of Canada, the protection of our homes, the persons living in those homes, in our towns and on the farms is an obligation of the federal government. It is the duty of the government to be prepared to meet any onslaught or any attack that might possibly be made by any potential enemy. While the war may be in Europe or Asia or in our own country, the object of our participation in it is based on the same principle, namely, the defence of Canadian homes and the Canadian way of life.
Civil defence fits into this picture. It is actually indivisible from the over-all picture. Again I say, although it is localized in municipalities and with provincial governments,
fMr. Jones.]

it is still the obligation of the federal government to provide the funds for civil defence. At the present time the participation of the municipalities is on a voluntary basis, and is auxiliary to the general plan. The participation of the hard-pressed municipalities should be restricted entirely to the providing of personnel. The funds should come from parliament, and they should be a direct charge on the $5 billion program that this government proposes to pass at this session.
I would suggest that as a first step toward making this body efficient, training classes should be held in our schools; that classes for civil defence, particularly in the higher grade schools, should be held previously, giving instructions to selected teachers during either the Easter recess or the summer recess, if that is soon enough, and training them to come back to their pupils, and help them to become part and parcel of the local civil defence in the town wherever they may happen to live. I know that this worked wonders in England during the blitz, because they had something of the nature of trained personnel in all localities.
I agree with hon. members who have already spoken that the first step that should be taken is a program of national registration. I believe that is urgent. In spite of the fact that it has been said it cannot be done, I should like to see an effort made to combine national registration of this type with the census. In England only through national registration were they able to determine how many people lived in a certain blitzed house. After they had counted the number rescued the list showed that there were two or three others still unaccounted for. They went on and worked until all were accounted for. In Canada, particularly in Ottawa, I doubt whether the residents living in an apartment house themselves know how many people are living there. They definitely do not know all the names. In the event of aggression and, shall we say, demolition of one of these apartment houses, we would be at a total loss to know how long to go on searching the ruins for the injured and killed, no registered list being available.
I also feel that help should be given the municipalities to provide fire fighting equipment. In the matter of providing fire fighting equipment the same problem is facing the municipalities as is facing the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), namely, lack of standardization. I would suggest that now is the time, if any help is given by the federal government to the municipalities to provide fire fighting equipment, to see that they have standardized couplings, connections and so on, on all the equipment supplied so that

that equipment could be transferred to another community that might be in difficulties and needed it. Until that is done I am afraid that the equipment in some towns in Canada would be totally unsuitable for other towns, because there is no standardization of couplings and connections.
I do not believe that the question of civil defence calls for secrecy. I do not believe it calls for the secrecy that naturally the general defence of the country demands. I believe that publicity is essential in this instance, a full knowledge of the gravity of the situation, and a full knowledge of the part that our citizens are expected to play in the event of a catastrophe. With the facts known you will get greater co-operation, and people will be willing to take their part and meet their obligation to the community.
Hospital supplies should be checked immediately to make sure that they are adequate for any eventuality. Food supplies should be placed in cold storages. I have in mind the fact that last year one of our British Columbia communities was cut off for a matter of two or three weeks, and it was completely out of food. That was not one isolated case. That could happen in any community in Canada, because few communities carry more than two or three weeks' supply of food at any given time in their cold storages. We should encourage merchants, wholesalers and all food suppliers to put large quantities of food in cold storage at the present time as part of our civil defence. I hold in my hand a publication issued by the government dealing mainly with ways and means of combating it in the event that aggressive war should be directed at Canadian targets. On reading it I find that it missed one important point, and that important point in my opinion is the possible sabotage that may follow aggres;-sion by a potential enemy, in this case Russia.
We know that in our midst there are men who would carry out a program of sabotage to assist the enemy immediately. Probably they are not numerous, but we have them. Possibly they are scattered all over this dominion ready to play their part, not for Canada but for a possible enemy. Men of this type can do more damage in a month or so to the economy of the country than can an aerial attack, by damaging the water, light, power and sanitation systems. I suggest that that matter be given serious consideration and included in this book for the information of the people who are making use of this as a basis of civil defence.
I find that the municipalities in British Columbia are willing to co-operate in every way they can; but with the high cost of education, hospitalization, social services and 80709-265
The Address-Mr. Jones other commitments, they definitely have not the money and they are looking to the government for help.
In this booklet there is a chapter dealing with one important matter, namely, the dispersal of industry. I believe not only in the dispersal of industry, but in the dispersal of population, as they offer the poorest target to any enemy aircraft that may come to this country. I would urge the government to use its influence now with these departments that are spending a billion dollars, when they ask the industry to accept a contract, or a contract is given. If it has to start a new plant it should be asked to try and find a location in Canada where it would help the local conditions and where it would become dispersed.
I could tell of several areas in British Columbia, hidden in the mountains where no enemy could find them. Near towns such as Penticton, Kelowna, Vernon and Grand Forks would be ideal for industries of this nature. I would not say this would include industries calling for 10,000 or 20,000 men; but industries calling for anything from 100 to 1,000 men could be ideally located both as to the availability of power and manpower, and protection from potential enemies.
If the government is going to take part in establishing a steel industry in British Columbia I would suggest that it give consideration to what is known as the Princeton area. In that area are found some of the largest coal deposits in British Columbia, as yet untouched. The mines there have been operating for about thirty years, and up to this date only about 4 per cent of the known coal has been mined. About 96 per cent of the coal in that area is still available. This affords cheap power, and to my mind would be ideal for the establishment of a steel industry.
In line with the suggestion by my hon. friend, that this debate affords opportunity to place local problems before the house, I would draw the attention of the government to the recent floods in the Fraser valley and in my own riding at Princeton. Our valleys, because they are valleys, are conducive to flood conditions. At the same time they offer means of control by way of dams. Such controls are not possible on the prairies.
Three years ago the Okanagan valley suffered a severe flood. It was so alarming that the government took steps to remove the possibilities of a recurrence. A commission of engineers was appointed, and it came to the conclusion that controls were feasible and possible. With that in mind the commission made recommendations to the government,

The Address-Mr. Jones and money has been provided in the estimates. However, the work has not yet commenced. This year in that valley we are particularly alarmed by the potential danger of similar floods in the current year. We understand that the lack of government action has been caused in one instance through not having been able to negotiate the purchase of land from Indians. I believe that could be overcome. The difficulty in the other case was through having to supply fish ladders at the request of the state of Washington. This, too, can be overcome. I would ask the government to speed the work. The people whose lands and homes are subject to these floods have been waiting anxiously for the government to implement its promise. I realize it is possibly too late to help to stem floods in the natural way, because we have been logging fairly heavily the territory that supplies the moisture which causes the floods. The denuding of the land has possibly added to the condition from which we suffer. At the same time the silted river outlets retard the flow, and a crooked river has to be straightened out. All this is known to the government, through its engineers.
I suggest to the government it would be far cheaper to have this work done now, because if the money is not now spent and if the work is not carried out the damage that may be caused, through a flood similar to that of three years ago, would cost the government more money by way of compensation than would be required to carry out this work at the present time.
One other matter I would draw to the attention of the government has to do with our fruit industry. I do not know whether hon. members are fully aware of the value of the British Columbia fruit industry to the economy of Canada. For the information of the house I shall place on record some figures showing the growth of the industry. In 1920 we shipped 43,000 tons of fruit and vegetables from the valley. This was contained in 2,600 carloads. In 1949 we shipped 258,600 tons, or 16,162 carloads. The freight revenue to the railways from these shipments, during the same period of time, had increased from half a million dollars to $8,500,000, plus the increased inbound traffic.
Employees in this industry have grown in number, i.e., in the packing houses, shook mills, processing plants and so on from less than a thousand in 1920 to over 8,000 in 1949. During that period payrolls jumped from $300,000 to between $8 million and $9 million. I am bringing these matters to the attention of the house because this prosperous industry received a severe shock last winter, caused by the frost-something which


is most unusual in our part of Canada. That frost took a toll of 336,610 trees. I am giving the correct figure, because the information was secured through a count made under the auspices of the provincial government. The average loss would be about 20 per cent. Some districts lost as much as 54 per cent, and some individual growers lost 100 per cent of their trees. The over-all loss to growers can best be shown by referring to specific fruits such as peaches, cherries, apricots, pears, plums and prunes. The crop sold in 1949 for $7,484,874 while in 1950, after the loss, it sold for $1,832,691. In other words the crop loss, exclusive of apples, was $5,652,183.
These people are not asking for compensation for that loss; they are asking for assistance, and I believe assistance is now being negotiated between the provincial and federal governments, and consideration is being given as to what assistance they will or can provide. I hope the federal government will go out of its way to show its desire to rehabilitate these men on the land and make them once again prosperous taxpayers, as they once were. This applies particularly to those who suffered to the extent of 50 or 100 per cent. As I said, these people are not asking for charity; they are asking for compensation to replace trees, and for long-term loans to cover replanting, living costs, fixed charges, taxes, irrigation, spraying and the like.
Hon. members perhaps know that it takes eight years to bring an orchard to the point of bearing. These people are willing to bring their orchards to that point, if they can be financed during that eight-year period. They would like to get loans through one of the government agencies at 2 or 2J per cent. This would re-establish, not newcomers to Canada but experienced farmers, farmers who have had twenty or thirty years' experience in the growing of fruit. This form of help would rehabilitate men who have contributed to the country, and who still have something to contribute to the economy of this dominion. Many of them are veterans; some are veterans of the first world war and they have been badly hit. Farmers in other parts of Canada have been rehabilitated in the past, and I do not think we would be breaking new ground if in this case the government saw fit to assist the farmers of the Okanagan valley.
Naturally this disaster has definite results on the workers, many of whom worked part time as pickers, thinners and general orchard workers. These people go to the packing houses for part of the year, and while there they are called upon to pay unemployment insurance. But they do not pay this when

they are on the farm and the combined period does not permit them to benefit under the act. The industry is having difficulty in getting help and one reason is that many men are leaving the farms because farm work offers no protection for the worker. This particular organization, possibly the largest in Canada, the British Columbia Fruit Growers Association, was asked to support a resolution produced by the workers asking that they be afforded the benefit of unemployment insurance. I think their claim is fair and just and I should like to place this resolution on the record. It originated in Peach-land and reads:
Whereas employees in most industries are now covered by unemployment insurance, and agricultural workers are not, and
Whereas this has the effect of sending the more responsible type of worker from the land to other industries with the consequent tendency not only to lower the standard of farm help available but also to make farm help increasingly difficult to secure:
Therefore be it resolved that this 1951 B.C.F.G.A. convention request the federal government to make unemployment insurance available to agricultural workers in cases where such workers desire to be covered by this insurance.
I understand there are certain difficulties that would have to be overcome in connection with extending the benefits of unemployment insurance to farm workers, and one difficulty is caused by the nature of the industry. The farms are scattered all across the dominion and it would be quite difficult for the auditors to carry on their work. One suggestion has been made, which I endorse, that when farmers come under the scheme on a voluntary basis they should be [DOT] willing to agree, and I am quite sure they would, to bring their books to a central point at a given time each year for auditing, possibly the nearest town.
One other matter I should like to refer to before I close is the Vernon campsite. Last summer I visited this campsite once or twice and the people in the district asked me, and I think quite rightly, why the Canadian government had sent troops to be trained at Fort Lewis. Fort Lewis and the area surrounding is all flat country, almost like the prairies, while the terrain around Vernon is hilly, and in many respects similar to the terrain of Korea. It would be ideal for training when the conditions are so similar.
In addition the climate is excellent and the facilities are already there. Light and water is available and sanitation facilities. Thousands of troops were trained here during the last war and all these facilities are available today. I understand that roughly 9,000 men were sent to Fort Lewis and the government is paying a premium at the rate of $40 per month for officers and $20 per month for
The Address-Mr. Green men. On the basis of 1,000 officers and 8,000 men it means that Canada is paying a premium of $200,000 per month in order to have men trained at Fort Lewis, and that is in addition to the pay and other expenditures that are being expended in United States dollars which a few months ago we were told were so scarce that they had to be withheld from ordinary industrial ventures.
The government should consider bringing these men back to Canada to complete their training, and I suggest that they be sent to Vernon because I know it is suitable. I suggest they be brought back before this extra cost of $200,000 a month accumulates and takes too large a bite out of our $5,000 million program.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subamendment under debate seeks to add a paragraph to the amendment which was moved the other day by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). The new paragraph would read as follows:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed
4. To ensure that a complete program of preparedness including compulsory training in the reserve forces for home defence be executed with the greatest possible degree of equality of sacrifice and service.
That subamendment contains three parts. First of all it stresses preparedness and the necessity of a complete program for that purpose. Secondly, it includes, as only one aspect of that preparedness, compulsory training in the reserve forces for home defence. Thirdly, it contains a very important reference to equality of sacrifice and service. I propose to divide my remarks this evening into three similar parts.
I believe that this is one of the most important amendments that have come before this House of Commons in the fifteen years I have been privileged to be a member representing one of the seats in the western city of Vancouver. I may say at the beginning that it is my intention to support the subamendment. I give credit for honesty of purpose to all hon. members who have spoken on this amendment, including those who belong to my own party, and also any hon. members who will be speaking before the vote is taken. All I ask is that I be given the same credit.
There is room for various opinions in discussing the subjects raised by this subamendment. I believe that those subjects are better discussed now than after war begins. We can debate them calmly and with reason. There is no excuse for bitterness or tension in a debate on this amendment at the present


advocates and what the Canadian Legion advocate is that the units of the reserve forces be brought up to strength by compulsory service. That is an entirely different thing.
Here again I suggest that the government set the number and the kind required, choose them by lot from the groups best fitted to serve, and let others volunteer if they wish to do so. In that way we shall get in our reserve forces the men best able to do the job. Operational units, such as our anti-aircraft regiments, our radar units and our coast defence regiments wiT be able to fulfil their functions. The men in the reserve army will get at least partial training; and how important training was when the Department of National Defence were trying to get young Canadians to enlist for the special service force! I have here in my hand their advertisement of August 8, 1950. The words printed across the bottom are as follows:
Armed aggression must be met with trained united strength.
That was true then and it is even more true today; and it applies to the reserve forces as well as to the active forces. Taking the action I suggest would certainly cut down the time in which these reserve units could get into action; and time is of the essence in this business of fighting a war in 1951. It would also give the reserve units a chance to do their job, and that job is to defend Canada.
Arguments have been made about the practicability of such a plan. I believe that the men in the Legion have just about as good an idea as anybody in Canada as to what is or what is not practicable in the matter of defending this country. There you have a body of Canadians who are just as responsible in their thinking and in their action as any group of Canadians in the nation, including the group sitting here in the House of Commons. These men of the Canadian Legion do not take steps without the most careful consideration or without believing that the steps they are advocating are right. The fact that they have advocated such a step in itself shows the practicability of that step. There are others whom one might call in support of the practicability of this measure. I have here a press dispatch from Victoria, dated February 3 of this year. It is headed "Call-up Ruling Bad News for Reserve Unit" and reads as follows:
Disappointment was expressed in reserve army circles here today over the government's decision there will be no call-up of young men to fill the badly under-strength reserve battalions of this area,
"If that's the way it is, we'll just have to continue as best we can and hope voluntary enlistments will resume at the January rate," said Lt. Col. Walter Mosedale, commander of the First battalion, the Canadian Scottish Regiment (Princess Mary's).

We hope, however, the government will see fit to provide some additional compensation to make the reserve army more attractive to young men.
Then I have another witness here, namely Major-General M. H. S. Penhale, C.B.E., C.B., who has been the general officer commanding western command, and has now retired. He was questioned about this Legion plan less than a month ago. In fact, the press dispatch is dated just one month ago tonight. Here is what he had to say:
"There are so many competing interests and activities, it is difficult to persuade men to devote their time to the reserve."
General Penhale said he supported the Canadian Legion stand for compulsory military training in the reserve force.
"Every other country has had to come to compulsory training. I don't know why we should he privileged," he said.
His statement to the other Vancouver evening paper was to the same effect. The dispatch reads as follows:
Canada's reserve army needs more men, says Major-General M. H. S. Penhale, retiring general officer commanding western command.
Interviewed here on his farewell visit to Pacific coast military units, the army chief declared: "I am in favour of any scheme that will fill up the ranks of the reserve force."
Asked if he favoured the Canadian Legion plea for compulsory military training service for all Canadian youth, he replied indirectly:
"Just about every other country has had to come to this."
Then there is the submission made by the conference of defence associations. Portions of that have been read by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness). I do not intend to read all of it this evening, but there are one or two portions which I think should be read to this house. These are statements by the men who are responsible primarily for the reserve army of Canada:
The threat of war has never been greater. The need for strength if war is to be averted and to meet that danger if it comes is recognized by every democratic country in the world, including our own. It is admitted that to successfully prosecute a war against our potential enemies will take every effort the free countries of the world can put forth. Every country of the Atlantic pact, with the sole exceptions of Canada and Iceland, has adopted some form of selective service. In all these countries, including our own, vast sums are to be spent on the armed services.
Reserve units have been asked to recruit to strength, if possible. The need for strong reserve units is therefore recognized.
Years of experience have taught us all that to obtain anything like the number of men now required in the reserve force by voluntary means is impossible. Large sums have been spent on advertising and in other ways to induce men to join the reserve force. To a large extent, such moneys have been wasted. The men have not been and are not coming forward.
The men represented through the conference have exhausted every effort to improve these conditions and have sacrificed time and their own money in such efforts.
The Address-Mr. Green The delegates to the conference feel that, since the effectiveness and efficiency of the reserve force is largely their responsibility, and that of the men they represent, they would be derelict in their duty to the government and to their fellow countrymen if they did not put before that government and the people of Canada their views as to the present state of the reserve force.
Then they go on to deal with the fact that we are not getting value for our money, and continue:
In spite of the existing shortages of facilities for the reserve force, in many places the strength of units does not absorb present facilities for training by a substantial margin. Far more men could be trained in the reserve force than are presently coming forward.
The turnover of other ranks is such that the vast majority of men who appear from time to time on the nominal rolls of reserve force units receive no training worthy of the name. They do not stay with the unit long enough. To say that the reserve force is 40,000 strong, and to give the Canadian people the idea that it has 40,000 men who could quickly be ready for action, is a travesty of the facts. There are few, if any, reserve units in Canada that could be ready to function in action under a minimum period of six months. This includes anti-aircraft and other such units which should be ready for immediate action. The Canadian public, in spite of the moneys spent, cannot look to effective and efficient protection from internal sabotage or external aggression from its reserve force for a considerable period after war breaks out, and the active force is far too small to undertake the full burden of such duties.
The modern army, with modern equipment, requires vast numbers of men specially trained. These men are termed tradesmen or specialists. The shortage of such men, most of whom require many months of training, in addition to their ordinary training as soldiers, is almost total in the Canadian reserve force-and there is not the slightest hope of producing the numbers required under the present voluntary system.
They go on to point out:
If it is not to be Canadian policy to lean on our allies in the initial stages of a war-and we are satisfied that the national pride of our people will tolerate no such situation-then men must be made available for training now.
This will involve a national registration system and the introduction of an enforceable and enforced system of selective service for the reserve force. Only in this way will the reserve force obtain the men it needs, the training it must have, and the effectiveness which the Canadian people are entitled to expect in view of the expenditures involved. Only in this way can we build a reserve force to which Canada can look with confidence.
The minister offers no other way. In his speech the other evening he did not answer this question as to how reserve forces were to be raised. By the way, I also have a clipping from the dominion executive of the Naval Officers Association of Canada setting out that the situation in the naval reserve is much the same. The minister offers no other way. In other words, the government is failing to ensure preparedness for Canada, and if for no other reason I would vote for this amendment in an attempt to force some action by the government.

The Address-Mr. Goode
The third part of the subamendment is equality of sacrifice and service. That means equality of sacrifice and service in fighting, in dying; equality in preparing to defend Canada, and equality as between the men in the forces and the civilians, and do not forget that we are now in a time when prices are running wild. I believe it will be far more difficult to prevent profiteering in the years immediately ahead than it was during the last world war.
In 1939 when this house met on the outbreak of war a determination was expressed by practically every hon. member who spoke, that there must be equality of sacrifice and service, referring particularly to the men in the forces and the civilians. In this debate practically no mention has been made of that principle. No plans have been envisaged which keep that principle in mind. I think it is a very significant thing, and a very tragic thing, that there has not been more emphasis placed on equality of sacrifice and service. That is a policy which must be kept always in our minds and before the Canadian people.
Today there is far too much of the attitude that this is somebody else's war in Korea, some other country is in danger, not Canada. There is far too much of that attitude. This house and the Canadian people are not yet facing realities, although today young Canadian lads in the Princess Pats are moving up the frozen dirt roads of Korea to the battle line, going to what for many of them means death.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last few days we have listened to two members of the Legion offer two different ideas; one has just resumed his seat, the other was the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). Yesterday, the hon. member for Nanaimo spoke as a great Canadian. He also, although he did not know it until this moment, is a former officer-commanding of mine in the second world war. Since listening to his ideas yesterday and the ideas of the hon. member for Vamicouver-Quadra tonight, the latter speech based on half a dozen newspaper clippings, the other hon. gentleman speaking from his own experience, I am willing to go along with my former O.C.
Much is being made of this idea of compulsory service in the reserve force. I am speaking only about the Vancouver situation. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said that the Seaforths had the equipment for 900 men. I know that at Bessborough, for instance, which was the headquarters of my old regiment, you could perhaps put 250 men on parade, but I certainly could not have done any training at that time. The hon. 
member for Nanaimo knows the place very well. Where are these men that you are going to call into the reserve force going to be trained? I can say from the artillery angle perhaps better than any other that it takes at least two years to put a man on a twenty-five pounder and train him properly. You cannot do it in less time. They tell us here that three nights a week with two hours a night can train men for the defence of Canada. Three nights a week and two hours a night mean thirty days of training in a year. In thirty days in the last war we just about got a man ready to be able to put his hat on properly and find out where the cookhouse was, and perhaps he knew how to wear his uniform properly, and that is all the time we had.
During the last war I was in the instructional cadres of most of the training centres in Canada, and on coast defence, and I think it can be said that you cannot train men on part-time service. We have seen reserve forces go out with the twenty-five pounders on the coast and, with all due respect to them, while they do a very good job 1 doubt very much whether they would be much use in Korea.
There is only one way to get men into the army and to train them properly. The Prime Minister said the other day that when the time comes action, and proper action, will be taken. The proper action at that time, if we need men, is compulsory service, conscription, or whatever you wish to call it; and that is what I am in favour of, at the proper time. This compulsory service in the reserve force was perhaps a fine idea to put in a brief to present to the government, but I do not think there is any effectiveness to it.
I am a member of the Legion; but I still believe that it was ill-timed for the Legion to present this idea before they knew the government's program at this session. The subamendment asks the house to approve of reserve forces for home defence. I think I want to go a little further than did the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) the other night, when he spoke about the forces that were introduced into military service during the last war. He did not know it at the time, but I know now whom to blame for giving me the job of trying to take some of these home defence men and make them active. Perhaps some day I will be able to get back at him. That was one of the most disgraceful episodes in the history of the Canadian army, when we took men in the home defence force under the universal training idea and gave them the status of home defence troops, at one time not even giving them the privilege of putting "Canada" on their sleeves. I

remember that in Petawawa they walked down one side of the street and we walked down the other side, because we had a little badge on our arms with the letters "G.S.", and they were not permitted to use it. That was the caste system in the lower ranks of the army; and we do not want that back again.
If we are going into a war-perhaps some of the higher officers know, but it is not known to the backbenchers-let us go into it right. Let us go into it with that equality of service mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). If my boy has to go into the army, let him go in on the same basis as any other boy. Let the government take the lead and put him in the army, if we need him; but let my boy be on the same status as anybody else.
I am going to speak for only a moment longer. Let me congratulate the Legion upon at least bringing the need for preparedness to the attention of the country. I think their idea with respect to the reserve force should not be supported, and I told them that in Vancouver. So far as the Social Credit party is concerned, I think the subamendment is something that should have been thought about longer than evidently they did think about it. I intend to vote against it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just preceded me has referred to some of the policies carried out during the last war regarding manpower. I would agree with him that many of those policies deserve severe criticism. I would say further that some of them were absolutely despicable. But who put in those policies? The Liberal government did.
Let me remind the house of one or two things that were done. I remember how men were asked to be willing to volunteer for four months' training. They were definitely promised that at the end of that four months they would be allowed to return to their occupations. After the government got those men into the forces they were frozen there, and the government would not let them go back to their jobs. In other words they obtained those men under false pretences.
That has nothing to do with this subamendment, but it was Liberal policy. Then again I would agree that the kind of campaign which has been described as a zombie campaign, that was used in order to try and force men in the reserve army to go active, was also despicable. That, too, was government policy. It was the policy of the Liberal party.
I would say that if anything like that ever happened again, any officer responsible for carrying out such a policy should be disciplined. I realize that any member who
The Address-Mr. Quelch desires to vote against this subamendment will find it quite easy to make an excuse. So far however I have been struck by the weakness of the excuses that have been made. For example the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) stated that he supported the stand of the Legion but that he could not support the subamendment because it would mean something different, that it would mean setting up a different army. It is strange that he is the only man in the House of Commons who has come to that conclusion. Every other member who has spoken has recognized that our proposal is based upon the recommendation of the Canadian Legion. That was made clear when the subamendment was moved, and it has been made clear by every member of this group who has spoken. It has been clearly understood by other members in the house. Yet he, through some mysterious functioning of his mind, has jumped to the conclusion that this would set up an entirely different arm of the reserve army.
Let me read the subamendment, so that there may be no misunderstanding about it:
To ensure that a complete program of preparedness including compulsory training in the reserve forces for home defence be executed with the greatest possible degree of equality of sacrifice and service.
Those words "compulsory training in the reserve forces" are the exact words used in the Legion's program, "operation preparedness". In order that there should be no misunderstanding on the point we have pointed out that we were putting it forward in the same way that the Legion was putting it forward.
It has been stated by some members that they agree with the general proposal to have compulsory training in the reserve army, but that they think the timing is wrong. They do not think it is wise to bring it up at this time. I would say that that depends largely on the seriousness of the international situation, and how great a degree of urgency there may be. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), when he spoke in the house, gave a very graphic description of the international situation, after describing the situation in China and in Korea, went on to say that at present there are a large number of danger spots in the world, and he made reference to Indo-China, Malaya, Indonesia and Burma, and stated that if those countries came under the control of the communists India and Pakistan would be in a precarious position. He referred to the fact that both Persia and the Middle East were vulnerable, and also stressed the danger to Yugoslavia. Then he said that the danger to the free world is still greatest in western

The Address-Mr. Quelch Europe, and that we are now entering the period of the greatest danger, in the months ahead.
I think he made it quite clear that the situation in the world today is a very serious one. In his speech at Montreal the other day he mentioned the need for making haste. I would say that, with this picture in mind, and the knowledge that in Canada we have a very small population, considering the vast area over which that population is scattered, long lines of communication, great productive capacity, and great productive plants that have to be handled by this population, we should be careful indeed about the type of agreement that we sign under article 43 of the United Nations charter. If we sign agreements under that article of the charter by which we may be called upon to send forces to any part of the world where an act of aggression has been committed against a member of the United Nations we may find it impossible to meet our commitments under the North Atlantic treaty or to defend adequately our country against aggression, and of course, still further, to develop the resources of the country.
I regard the international situation today as being even more serious than the situation in either 1914 or 1939. I say that because the armed manpower against us is far more heavily weighted than it was on either of those former occasions. As is clearly pointed out in an article that appeared in the June issue of United Nations World headed in large letters, "Urgent" and with the subheading, "Memorandum on the Russian Military Power", Russia has 30,000,000 trained soldiers. The article continues:
Russia is convinced of its invincibility, of the absolute superiority of the red army over the armies of the capitalist world. All the people living under Russian rule are prepared ideologically and politically for war. Russia today has the strongest army in the world-about 170 infantry, 35 armoured and 60 artillery divisions. The peacetime strength of the red army amounts to 41 million men. The trained reserves are 25 milion. It can therefore lead into battle 30 million men.
And again:
The infantry is 60 to 70 per cent motorized, the artillery up to 80 per cent motorized.
In referring to armaments the article has this to say about tanks:
One should not repeat the mistake of underestimating Russian armament capacity. This mistake proved the doom of Germany. One must reckon on over 100,000 first-class tanks. The plants in Stalingrad alone produced in 1942 5,500 T-34's.
And finally:
In short, the Russians have at their disposal first-class weapons of their own manufacture. The American supplies in armaments were hardly noticeable during the war. At the front, only the

American trucks played an important part, but in the last few years Russia has expanded its production in this field too.
That indicates clearly the strength today of the armed forces of Russia, and it must be remembered that that article was written in June of last year. The article points out that the Russian air force is inferior to ours, but since June of last year Russia has greatly expanded its production of jet planes. These planes compare favourably with ours in the field although up to date the pilots have not proved to be as efficient.
Russia has no navy but, on the other hand, it has a strong submarine fleet. I think most people will agree that that is the only kind of fleet that Russia would require in the type of war she would probably be waging.
Therefore I say that there is no doubt that a very real danger exists. If war comes between the United States of America and the U.S.S.R. it is well to remember that Canada could not escape the consequences. When the defence minister outlined the defence program he stated, and I quote from page 97 of Hansard of February 5, 1951, as follows:
Meeting these manpower requirements is going to require a big effort and the wholehearted support of all sections of the population.
In this program the main emphasis is being placed on the air force, and I think rightly so. The program calls for only a moderate expansion of the active" army. Therefore I think it is essential that the reserve army be thoroughly reorganized and strengthened because it is bound to have an important role to play in the next world war if we are unfortunate enough to run into one.
I notice that many people, including men in the forces, older generals and** others, suffer from what might be called a European complex. They recall that in world war I and world war II the fighting was mainly in Europe and mostly between European nations. But if there is a third world war the situation will be entirely different. Such a war would not be between European nations, it would be between the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R., with Canada sandwiched right in between the two countries. Many people have stated that in the event of another war Canada might well be the Belgium of that war.
That being the case I think it is obvious that the reserve army will play a most important role in helping to maintain our anti-aircraft defences and in preventing acts of sabotage across the country. No one in this house has stressed the importance of the reserve army more than the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), and he has done it most effectively. I should like to quote a statement made by the leader of the opposition

with reference to the reserve army, and I direct the attention of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) to the fact that this speech was made after the minister of defence had spoken and not before. The leader of the opposition is reported on page 287 of Hansard of February 12 as follows:
No one should underestimate the importance in the Canadian defence plan of the reserve army. One of the things that have not been answered in the debate, but which should be answered, is the statement by the senior officers of all the associations representing the different branches of the land forces, that any suggestion that the number of men we have in the reserve is an effective force for the defence of this country is a travesty of the facts. These men who made that statement are the men who know best of all what the state of training of the reserve units really is. They know better than the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). They know better than the general staff. They know better than anyone else because they are the ones who are actually assuming responsibility for that training. They have made the bald statement that we are not getting full value for our money in reserve training, and that any statement that we have 40,000 effectives, which has been made over and over again, is a travesty of the facts.
It is interesting to note what those men have suggested in the way of methods by which the reserve army could be made more effective. I should like to quote from the report of the brief of the conference of defence associations published in The Legionary for February, 1951. The extracts read as follows:
Years of experience have taught us all that to obtain anything like the number of men now required in the reserve force by voluntary means is impossible. Large sums have been spent on advertising and in other ways to induce men to join the reserve force. To a large extent such moneys have been wasted. The men have not been and are not coming forward.
If it is not to be Canadian policy to lean on our allies in the initial stages of a war-and we are satisfied that the national pride of our people will tolerate no such situation-then men must be made available for training now. This will involve a national registration system and the introduction of an enforceable and enforced system of selective service for the reserve force. Only in this way will the reserve force obtain the men it needs, the training it must have, and the effectiveness which the Canadian people are entitled to expect in view of the expenditures involved. Only in this way can we build a reserve force to which Canada can look with confidence.
Note that the conference of defence associations insists that there must be some form of compulsory selective service in order to maintain the reserve army up to strength. Mind you, this is the opinion of the men who the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) states know better than anybody else, and his statement to that effect was made after the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) had spoken. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) states that such a policy would discourage men from enlisting. I find it hard to follow that reasoning. I cannot see why,
The Address-Mr. Quelch just because we might have some form of compulsory training of the reserve army, men would stop enlisting in the active service force. I would say that if anything it might have the opposite effect. At least those men who went overseas would have the satisfaction of knowing that we were training men at home to defend this country in case of an act of aggression, and in leaving their families at home there would be a better chance of their being defended than if we had no defence force at all.
The hon. member for Nanaimo referred to shortage of equipment and suggested that it is useless to bring men into the reserve army if we have not the equipment with which to train them. Again I should like to refer to a statement appearing in the same issue of The Legionary quoting a statement by the Minister of National Defence. It reads:
In a statement to the Canadian press Mr. Claxton said that compulsory service is "a matter for the government and parliament." He denied that equipment shortages are, as the Legion claims, a major obstacle to any program of enforced training in the reserves.
Again, when he spoke in the house, as recorded at page 94 of Hansard, he stated:
The Canadian army . . . has in store or on issue most of the equipment for four divisions, even more of some weapons . . .
Surely nobody can argue that we will not have the equipment to equip these men if we take them into the reserve army when, according to the Minister of National Defence, we have equipment stored away for four divisions. The hon. member for Nanaimo states that we have not got the facilities. Nevertheless we should remember that in many parts of Canada our facilities are not being used to their full capacity, and that very few of the reserve army units are up to full strength. He talked about taking in hundreds of thousands of men. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) dealt with that question. The Legion has never suggested universal training of that kind. They have called for national registration, and as a result of national registration the government would have sufficient information upon which to decide the number of men that should be trained. In taking men into the reserve army they would be very careful to see that they would not take them in at a faster rate than they had facilities with which to train them.
The hon. member for Nanaimo also talked about a number of difficulties being in the way of compulsory service. I am surprised that he of all people should talk about difficulties and suggest that just because we have difficulties we should not go ahead with compulsory training. In wartime we always
406	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Quelch face big difficulties but we overcome them. Surely nobody is going to suggest that we could not overcome the difficulties that would face us as a result of taking men into the reserve army. Remember that the men who are advocating this policy are the men who have been and are in charge of these units, officers' attending the conference of defence associations. Apparently they are quite confident that they can overcome any difficulties that may arise.
All members have received copies of the Legion program, "operation preparedness", so I am not going to go into details. I want to mention three points briefly. First of all there is the question of national registration which would provide the government with the information necessary to enable them to make the very best use of the manpower of the country. Second, there is the mobilization of industry for defence purposes. Again I think the reason for this is obvious. It would be for the purpose of bringing about maximum production of required goods. I think that in mobilizing our industrial resources we should do everything in our power to decentralize our industries. During the last war we unfortunately had a still greater concentration of industry in the east. If we are going to expand our industrial plants I think we should bring about decentralization as far as possible. We should try to build up regional zones and make them as selfsufficient as possible. In the last war one of the reasons Russia was able to fight back was that she had decentralized her industry. Therefore, as she was driven back, she had behind the Ural mountains industries that she was able to utilize. If all her industries had been concentrated in the areas that Germany conquered she might very well have been brought to her knees.
Then there is the question of compulsory training of men in the reserve forces. This would at least ensure that if an attack were made on Canada we would have men trained to defend the country, and also a source of reinforcements for the active forces. We believe that in the kind of world in which we are living today some form of compulsory training is absolutely essential. We believe that compulsory training in the reserve army would provide a maximum number of men with, at the same time, the least possible dislocation of industry. It is often stated that if a third war comes the enemy will move so fast we will not have time to train men. Fortunately the third war has not come yet. We still have time to train men, and it is up to us to see that we make the very best use of the time at our disposal to train men so that they will be in a position to defend 

Canada efficiently in the event of an attack, and in order that we may play a strong part under the North Atlantic treaty.
As I stated in the beginning, questions have been raised as to the timing and wisdom of this suggestion, for compulsory service. As far as time is concerned I would say we have already lost too much time and therefore should act as quickly as we can on this matter. As to its wisdom, if hon. members are suggesting that it would not be politically expedient then I would say that if the government would lay their cards upon the table face up I am satisfied the people of this country would be willing to make any sacrifice necessary in order that we in Canada might continue to be a free people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house for a few moments whilst I discuss a few matters I believe to be of importance. Let me begin with those famous first words: "I intend to be brief."
First I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr, McMillan) and seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on the able manner in which they carried out their difficult task. I do not know whether they have had previous experience in parliamentary debate, but they discharged the duty assigned to them in a manner worthy of veterans. Both hon. members represent very important constituencies and very honourable professions, the mover being a member of the medical fraternity and the seconder a member of the bar. Each was a leader in his profession in his own, community, and I am sure that in deciding to enter public life they realized, as some of us have come to realize, that they would be making a sacrifice. From their first efforts in this house, however, I am sure they will meet with success as servants of the people.
Before entering into a discussion of the topics I propose to deal with, I should like to pay tribute to three departed parliamentarians who were well known to a great many members of this house. I refer to the late members for Brandon, Queens, and Kindersley. All these gentlemen possessed noble qualities of soul and mind which endeared them to all who knew them, and many of our lives were in some measure enriched by the friendship we enjoyed with them. To their bereaved families I extend my deepest sympathy, and I am sure all hon. members who knew those gentlemen share my feelings.
We are passing through a very serious period in our history. We are called upon to make sacrifices, to practise self-denial,

to increase our material production, and especially to tighten our ranks so we may have that unity so essential in a crisis of this kind. We need have no fear. Our nation, which has gone through two great wars and emerged so successfully, can again cope with the situation and take its place beside the major powers of the world in the defence of democracy and liberty.
Domestically we possess all that is required to achieve these ends. We may, by great effort, increase our production for the benefit of all. On the international front I believe Canada is doing her share; and I am sure the efforts of our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) at Lake Success during the last two or three years have won the admiration of the Canadian people, more especially in the role he played lately when he attempted to obtain a cease-fire in Korea. He has risen in the esteem of our people, and has won a niche as one of the foremost statesmen of the world. In listening to him in this house the other day I am sure everyone appreciated that we had a minister of foreign affairs who can match anyone at Lake Success.
I confess that I have no profound knowledge of the intricacies of diplomacy or foreign affairs. I am but an amateur, like many others, and probably in speaking on these matters I am rushing in where angels fear to tread. Yet I must refer to certain policies adopted by the Atlantic pact nations, which we as a member of that pact must follow, which contain some contradictions. It is hard to follow the pattern of these foreign policies. We are justly proud of the fact that our own Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was the first to suggest the North Atlantic treaty alliance, but when it was suggested we had no doubt it would be difficult to bring together all the nations which needed the protection of such an alliance since some of them, including the Scandinavian countries and those we call the low countries, were so close to Russia they might be hesitant about joining such a pact. It was only after much persuasion that we were able to gather together the nations circling the north Atlantic; but many of us cannot understand why Spain was not included.
I agree with the suggestion made this afternoon by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) that we should try to bring Spain into this pact. We continue to treat Spain with disdain. We refuse her the right to participate in the deliberations under the North Atlantic pact. I was surprised the other day to read a dispatch in which Prime Minister Attlee was quoted as saying that Spain was not necessary, that Spain would not contribute anything if it
The Address-Mr. C. T. Richard joined the North Atlantic pact. Have we forgotten that Spain was the first nation in Europe to fight communism? If communism had been implanted in that important and strategic part of Europe, could we have won Italy against communism, as we did? We included Italy, a former enemy, in the North Atlantic pact, but we are denying Spain the same participation, and are even denying her a seat at Lake Success.
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) said this afternoon-and I quite share his opinion-that we need all the allies that we can get. Yes, indeed; in my opinion the free nations banded together in the North Atlantic pact need all the assistance, the friendship and the co-operation they can get from all the nations having the common concepts of Christian civilization which we have; I think especially of Spain. Probably we deplore the methods employed by Franco in achieving power; but were those methods any worse than those employed by the Russian regime, by Marshal Tito, or by any of those in power today in those countries which form part of the Russian bloc?
It seems to me that we have forgotten the sins of others but yet are not ready to cross the threshold of opportunity to bring about a rapprochement with Spain. I repeat that we need as many allies as we can get. Let us not forget that communism today controls one-third of the people of this earth and one-half of the area of the globe. Therefore it is important that we should have on our side all the democratic countries that we can gather together.
It is true that our relations with the South American countries are quite cordial. Yet I believe that they could be better. Probably we may not be able to say the same about the relations existing between that great country to the south of us and the South American countries. I can see no better way of bringing the countries of North and South America together than by recognizing Spain, which most of these South American countries regard as the mother country. Let us not forget that South America-and perhaps a good many do not know this-has a population of some 150 million people.
The spectre of communism is of such a grave character that the democratic countries cannot neglect any opportunity of winning friends to combat communism. We cannot remain complacent. We must throw away our prejudices. We must look at things from a different point of view. All means must be employed to fight communism, especially where it is sneaking in as it is both in this country and in the United States.

The Address-Mr. C. T. Richard
Behind the iron curtain today are millions of people who at one time possessed democratic governments and enjoyed freedom of worship. Of this great number some 50 millions in countries such as Hungary, Poland, Austria, Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, are Roman Catholics. These people never have and never can become communists no matter how long communism may have a stranglehold on the country. To them democracy cannot exist without religion and religion cannot exist without democracy; for both have a common ideal, a common cornerstone, as it were, namely the dignity of man. They realize that today the communist regimes have recognized the fact that their worst enemy is the church and that they must stifle and eradicate all religious beliefs amongst these people in order to win. The Reds plan the conquest of all religious life in Europe. The persecution of such intellectual lights and great religious leaders as Cardinal Mindszenty, Cardinal Beran and other Catholic prelates was not carried out because they wished to attack the Catholic church more than any other sect. Protestant leaders were also persecuted as well as Zionist leaders. It is quite evident that communism fights all sects and that communism feels that it cannot succeed as long as there is a certain religious belief in the hearts of the people. They have plainly made their intention known by a manifesto which was issued last July at Prague for the purpose of rallying the communists in their fight against the church. Let me read from that manifesto and let me point out these extraordinary things. The manifesto reads as follows:
The church -
And I would note here that no particular church is indicated; the word is general.
-is our greatest enemy. This enemy is centred in the peasantry-
I wish to note again here that no particular church is indicated where they say "peasantry", meaning thereby that that is where probably the religious belief is strongest; that is, in that class of society. The manifesto continues:
-and unless we liquidate this opposition we shall not be able to conquer resistance in the villages as to the establishment of co-operatives-
Meaning collectives.
-and completion of our socialist program. There the communist party must gain strong foundation in the villages.
It is quite clear that the communist regime of those countries behind the iron curtain wishes to destroy independence of worship and to extinguish the flame of democracy. It is therefore regrettable that this country has not yet seen fit to appoint an accredited representative to the Vatican where perhaps


more information may be obtained as to conditions behind the iron curtain than in any other capital in Europe. The Vatican is one of the outstanding diplomatic posts in the world today because of the large number of diplomats accredited to the Holy See, which numbers some 400 million adherents.
Let me assure the house that I do not make the suggestion because Rome or the Vatican happens to be the seat of the religion to which I adhere. Far from me be any such motive. I may say that I am prompted in bringing up this subject more by the fact that I happened to be in Rome a few months ago. I spent some time there. I had read much about the life that went on behind the iron curtain. While in Rome, amongst the thousands of visitors there during the Holy Year, I met hundreds of them. I had an opportunity to obtain information of what went on. Some of them came from countries behind the iron curtain, others from countries adjacent to it. They were people who had firsthand knowledge of conditions as they existed there. I was impressed with the great desire of these people, who are being subjected to communism, to keep a link with the western countries, and a desire for help to keep the flame of democracy alive and to keep the little liberty of worship they still possessed.
In suggesting that we should have a representative at the Vatican let me assure this house that I do not mean that he should be of any particular sect. In my estimation he should not be a representative at the Holy See because His Holiness is head of the Catholic church. He should be a representative at the Vatican because His Holiness is a sovereign in his own right, and that is the way he is recognized by nations who have accredited representatives there from the East where the Mohammedan religion dominates and where probably the Christian sects are very little known. They have representatives at the Holy See because His Holiness is a temporal ruler and not because he is the head of any particular church.
I know that there is still some opposition to our sending a representative to the Holy See under the false belief that it would be a recognition of a particular religion. But other countries do not view it in that light. Great Britain has had a representative at the Vatican for years, and the latest dispatches tell us that the United States will send one. Therefore we should regard it from another and more practical point of view. We should forget the religious part of it.
I believe that in this country we have reached a certain period in our history where we can see it is time to forget our petty differences and jealousies in matters of creed

or race. Every day I read of the great strides that this country is making in the development of our resources, in the expansion of our trade and of our wealth, and I am sure that other hon. members feel as I do as I read this every day. I feel proud of my country. I feel that it is the best in the world. It is well that we should be told of its great progress; but there is another sphere in which we have made progress in this country during the last twenty years, a progress which has been noticeable. I believe we have come to understand one another better. I believe there is not the ill feeling between races and creeds in this country that existed some twenty or twenty-five years ago. There may be some differences yet, but I believe we have made progress, and we should mention it.
Probably the two world wars which we have gone through have brought about this better feeling. Some call it tolerance. Lately I have come to realize that this word "tolerance" is abused an awful lot. Tolerance means to forbear, to forgive something which should not exist, to accept a necessary evil. I do not believe we should use the word "tolerance". In describing the better feeling which exists between the different races and creeds in this country we should call it respect for the ideas, the languages, the beliefs and the customs of others. To me that is more descriptive than tolerance.
According to the newspapers next week we celebrate brotherhood week. What better way could we observe it than by keeping in mind and trying to foster ways and means of coming to a better understanding of one another, bringing on a more intensified unity, a unity which is so essential today in this serious period of our history and the history of mankind.

I shall detain the house only five minutes in order to discuss a matter arising out of a question which I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon. The question had to do with the South Saskatchewan irrigation project. I do not think it is necessary at this "time for me to explain to most hon. members what that project is. It contemplates the building of a huge dam on the South Saskatchewan river in the dust bowl of my province. In the past, the Minister of Agriculture has been one of the strongest advocates of that project. There have always, however, been many excuses why it could not be started. A little more than a year ago, one of the minister's excuses was that provincial co-operation was not forthcoming in paying its share of the cost.
The Address-Mr. Thatcher
This afternoon I asked the minister whether the Saskatchewan government had agreed to pay $33 million toward the cost of the irrigation project, and his answer was:
I would rather say that I have a letter from the Saskatchewan government, in which they have urged that construction be proceeded with, and have agreed to take as a basis of discussion $33 million on the part of the provincial government, and the farmers and others who are interested, but I would not like to say that they have agreed to make that payment. It was merely suggested as a basis of discussion.
I do not know why the minister could not have given me a yes or no to my question. I do not know why he had to answer so ambiguously.

I will tell him now why,
because I had a letter from the premier in my hand, and that is what he said.

I must differ; what are the
facts about this irrigation project? The provincial government has always maintained, as I think most Liberal speakers have maintained until the C.C.F. came into power in Saskatchewan, that this irrigation project was primarily a federal project. We heard very little until about a year ago about the fact that the provincial government would be expected to pay a large portion of these costs.
In discussing his estimates on October 14, 1949, the minister made this statement, as reported in Hansard at page 812:
We must have assurances from somebody that an organization will be set up to utilize the water, and that they are going to contribute a share of the cost sufficient to ensure that they will take some responsibility for seeing that the work is carried on.
In other words, he went on to point out that the provincial government would have to pay a substantial share of the cost. We felt that this was not in the best interests of the nation, first of all because provincial revenues are so limited and, secondly, because the federal government has had such huge surpluses since the end of the war. It seemed obvious that the federal government, because the project was national in scope, should be able to proceed more satisfactorily. However, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has refused since that time to discuss the subject, except on the basis that the province would pay a substantial amount.
Finally, two weeks ago the minister went to Regina, I understand, and met the Saskatchewan government. They told him, in effect, that they still felt it was a federal responsibility. However, in order to get the project started, and in order to try to get the work under way, they were reluctantly prepared to bear a share of the costs. They asked for specific information as to what was involved.
410	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Thatcher
I understand that the province was told it would have to be responsible, first, for $19 million to build a distribution system; secondly, for an estimated $6 million for levelling the land-the water owners would pay part eventually-and, thirdly, for $8 million to instal hydroelectric installations. The federal government would pay $68 million for the dam. In others words, the federal government was asking the government of Saskatchewan to pay the staggering sum of $33 million. The Minister of Agriculture certainly threw down a challenge when he asked them to find that amount of money.
However, the provincial government was so anxious to see the work started that after much consideration, even though the costs involved were so heavy, even though they still thought the matter was a federal responsibility, and even though their revenues were limited, they decided they would proceed on the basis of the figure that was outlined to them by the Minister of Agriculture and his departmental officials. The premier of the province has made this specific commitment to the minister, as he mentioned in a letter a moment ago:
As soon as the federal government has announced its intention to proceed with this undertaking we are prepared to negotiate and sign an agreement on the basis of the allocation of costs outlined above.
In other words the provincial government is prepared to raise $33 million. How they will do it I do not know, but they are ready to go ahead with the project. They have agreed to the proposal, even though they think the terms are very severe. They are going to go along with it because they have to; they have accepted the minister's challenge.

What we want to know is this: In view of this commitment, when can the project be started? The Saskatchewan legislature is meeting at the present time, and I suppose the project would have to be endorsed, by that legislature. If so, why not without delay send the agreement out so that it can be ratified? I believe it would be passed unanimously. I suggest that the international situation is such, and the defence situation is such, that we should try to diversify our industry in a way that the building of this dam would


make possible. I would remind the house of what the Minister of Agriculture said a few years ago:
Development of irrigation and power on the South Saskatchewan river by means of the Outlook dam would mean industrial and agricultural development of western Canada similar to the Essen country of Germany.
Today we are facing the problem of inflation. We need greater production. Let us make an Essen in this part of western Canada, as the minister suggested. I believe that the citizens of Saskatchewan, whether they be Liberal, Conservative, or C.C.F., will be bitterly disappointed if, because of the international situation, the government decides to postpone this much needed work for a further period of time. I believe there is no major project needed as much in Canada today as this irrigation scheme, and in that statement I include the St. Lawrence seaway development.
